name: Professional laser hair removal

lead: Professional laser hair removal leaves skin smoother with far less regrowth on the face, neck, beard line and body. Users typically see regrowth cut by half or more over several visits.

A clinician passes a laser or intense pulsed light over the skin; the hair pigment absorbs the light and heats the follicle, damaging it. Wavelength and pulse length are matched to melanin while cooling protects the skin. Only follicles in the growth phase respond, which is why repeated sessions are needed. Under the FDA's definition, permanent means long-term reduction rather than total removal.

paras: Treatment is usually at least eight sessions spaced a few weeks apart, done in a clinic or medical spa. It shows best on dark hair and lighter skin; light, grey, red and fine hair respond poorly, and device choice matters for darker skin.

Short-term redness and swelling are common. More serious effects include burns, pigment changes, acne flares and infection, especially with the wrong device for the skin type. Rules for who may perform it vary by US state.

angle.text: Clinic lasers heat the pigment in hair so follicles are damaged and regrowth thins, typically by half or more over several visits. It gives smoother skin on the face, neck, beard line and body, and works best on dark hair and lighter skin.

lead: Professional laser hair removal is a clinic or medical-spa procedure in which pulses of laser or intense pulsed light heat the pigment in hair so that the follicle is damaged and regrowth is reduced. It is used on the face, neck, beard line, body and other areas, and is one of the most widely offered cosmetic hair-reduction treatments [1].

Wikipedia describes the principle as selective photothermolysis, with light of a chosen wavelength and pulse length absorbed by melanin in the hair while surrounding skin is largely spared. Under the FDA's definition the result is called permanent hair reduction, meaning a long-term stable reduction in the number of regrowing hairs rather than total removal [1].
infobox: Alexandrite 755 nm, diode 810 nm, Nd:YAG 1064 nm, ruby 694 nm, IPL [1]
Commonly eight or more, spaced about 3 to 8 weeks apart [1]
FDA regulates devices; practitioner rules set by states [1]

paras: Light absorbed by melanin heats the follicle's stem cells, and success depends on delivering enough heat for long enough. Pulse width is described as the most important parameter, with fluence measured in joules per square centimetre and larger spot sizes penetrating deeper. Contact, cryogen or cold-air cooling protects the epidermis, permits higher fluence and reduces pain [1].
Lasers act mainly on follicles in the active growth phase, so several sessions are needed. Treated hairs usually shed over two to three weeks [1].

Wikipedia lists ruby (694 nm, pale skin), alexandrite (755 nm, all skin types), pulsed diode array (810 nm, pale to medium skin), Nd:YAG (1064 nm, dark skin) and intense pulsed light (not strictly a laser, pale to medium skin). Argon lasers are no longer used [1]. The Nd:YAG with cooling has been used on dark skin by experienced practitioners, with some success [1].

The approach was tested experimentally for about 20 years before commercial release in 1995 to 1996. The FDA cleared it in 1997, and a 1998 Massachusetts General Hospital article was among the first published descriptions [1].

A 2006 review summarised by Wikipedia reported six-month hair reductions of about 69 percent for alexandrite, 72 percent for diode and 67 percent for IPL, with no significant short-term difference [1][2]. The same hair-removal article cites a 2006 Cochrane meta-analysis reporting about 50 percent reduction for up to six months with alexandrite and diode lasers and no evidence of reduction from IPL, Nd:YAG or ruby lasers [2]. An intrapatient trial cited in the laser article reported 52.7 percent reduction with IPL against 69.2 percent with diode laser at 12 months [1].

Results depend partly on operator skill and equipment. Light, red, grey, white and fine vellus hair respond poorly, and large areas often need touch-ups after an initial 3 to 8 treatments. Men's facial hair may need considerably more sessions [1]. Lasers can also treat pseudofolliculitis in people with coarse, curly facial hair [1].

Common effects such as itching, pink skin, redness and swelling usually last two or three days. The most common serious effects are acne flare-ups and skin discoloration; burns, hypopigmentation, scabbing, purpura and infection also occur. Numbing creams used over large areas have caused serious harm and even death, and allergic reactions to gels, numbing agents or early shaving are possible [1].

In the US the FDA regulates the devices, there is no federal practitioner licence, and almost all states regulate for-hire services; Florida, for example, requires commercial use by a physician or supervised clinician. As of 2025 some diode devices have been cleared for over-the-counter sale, and rules abroad vary [1].

Comparative studies of lasers and IPL for hair reduction are summarised above [1][2]. Separately, registered trials have tested laser hair removal for pilonidal disease, including a completed 22-person study [3] and a 302-person study of unknown status [4]; these concern a medical condition rather than cosmetic removal.
